tagline: Reading the inscriptions of pre-Roman Gaul — a two-stage epigraphic course in the continental Celtic tongue.
philosophy: Gaulish is known only from inscriptions: a few hundred texts carved in stone, cast in bronze, or scratched on lead. Full mastery is impossible. The corpus is finite, the grammar reconstructed, and the vocabulary incomplete. But the voices are real. These are the words of the Gauls before Caesar, before Romanization, before their language vanished. This course teaches you to read them.
duration_estimate: 2–3 months at one hour per day
method: Epigraphic. We begin with the scripts, the sounds, the alphabet variants. Then we read the inscriptions themselves, one by one, with full linguistic commentary. No paradigm tables before texts. The texts are the point.
prerequisites: Some prior study of Latin or Greek helps. The Gaulish inscriptions often use the Latin or Greek alphabet, and many are bilingual. Familiarity with Indo-European noun declension will ease the path.

stages.name: The Sound and the Sign
stages.subtitle: The scripts, the sounds, the letters of Gaulish epigraphy.
learning_outcomes: Read Gaulish texts written in the Greek alphabet (southern Gaul, c. 300–50 BCE).
Read Gaulish texts written in the Latin alphabet (central and northern Gaul, c. 100 BCE–200 CE).
Recognize and produce the rare Lepontic script (northern Italy and adjacent Alpine valleys, c. 600–100 BCE).
Pronounce reconstructed Gaulish with confidence: the vowels, the diphthongs, the consonant clusters, the lenition patterns.

lessons.title: The Scripts of Gaul
lessons.content: Gaulish was written in three alphabets: Greek (in the south, introduced by Greek colonists at Massalia), Latin (after Roman contact), and Lepontic (the oldest, used by the Lepontii and adjacent Celtic peoples in the Alpine zone). We survey all three and their distributions.

lessons.title: The Greek-Script Inscriptions
lessons.content: The Gaulish Greek alphabet has twenty-four letters, matching the Greek of Massalia (modern Marseille). Vowels: Α, Ε, Η, Ι, Ο, Υ, Ω. Consonants: Β, Γ, Δ, Ζ, Θ, Κ, Λ, Μ, Ν, Ξ, Π, Ρ, Σ, Τ, Φ, Χ. Some Gaulish sounds had no Greek equivalent and were approximated. We read a short votive inscription from Vaison-la-Romaine.

lessons.title: The Latin-Script Inscriptions
lessons.content: Most surviving Gaulish is written in the Roman alphabet. Gaulish inherited Latin letter shapes but used them for Gaulish phonemes. The digraph <ou> represents /u:/; <x> may be /ks/ or /ss/. We read a funerary inscription from Alise-Sainte-Reine.

lessons.title: The Lepontic Alphabet
lessons.content: The Lepontic script is an adaptation of the Etruscan alphabet, itself derived from Greek. It was used primarily in the inscriptions of Cisalpine Gaul. Thirteen consonants, five vowels. Right-to-left or left-to-right. We read the Prestino inscription (late 2nd century BCE), one of the longest Lepontic texts.

lessons.title: Gaulish Phonology
lessons.content: The reconstructed sound system. Vowels: short a, e, i, o, u; long ā, ē, ī, ō, ū. Diphthongs: ai, ei, oi, au, eu, ou. Consonants: stops p, t, k, b, d, g; fricatives s, x /h/; nasals m, n; liquids l, r; semivowels w, j. Lenition in compounds and after certain particles. Accent probably initial (unlike Latin and Greek).

lessons.title: Reading Drill: Names and Theonyms
lessons.content: Before we read sentences, we read names. The inscriptions are full of personal names (ANDEVDOS, SEGOMĀROS, EPOREDORIX) and divine names (LVGVS, ESVS, TARANIS, ROSMERTA, EPONA). These are the easiest entry points. We practice fifty of the most common.

lessons.title: Reading Drill: Formulae
lessons.content: Gaulish inscriptions repeat certain phrases: IEVRV (dedication formula), AVVOT (votive formula), and the common verb forms DEDEMIT (he gave), ETIC (and), ΟΥΕΙΛΛΟΝΜΑΡΚΟΝ (to Vello son of Marko). These chunks recur. Memorize them and you can read half the corpus.

checkpoint.title: Stage 1 Checkpoint
checkpoint.format: Written and oral. Twenty letters from each of the three scripts (Greek, Latin, Lepontic) to identify by name and sound; ten personal or divine names to read aloud and parse; five short inscribed phrases to transliterate and translate with glosses. Pass mark: 80%.

stages.name: The Reading
stages.subtitle: The inscriptions themselves, one by one.
learning_outcomes: Read and translate the Coligny Calendar with notes.
Read and translate the Larzac Tablet with notes.
Read and translate the Chamalières Tablet with notes.
Read and translate the Vercelli stone bilingual.
Read and parse ten funerary and ten dedicatory inscriptions.

Recognize the major morphological patterns: the -o- and -ā- stem nouns, the dative singular in -ui, the genitive in -i, the nominative plural in -es, the verb endings -it (3rd sg.) and -ont (3rd pl.).

lessons.title: The Coligny Calendar, Part One
lessons.content: The longest Gaulish text. A bronze tablet discovered in 1897 near Coligny (Ain, France), dating to the late 2nd century CE but recording a pre-Roman lunisolar calendar. Sixteen columns, sixty-two months over five years, with intercalations. The month names: SAMONIOS (summer-end), DVMANNIOS (dark-half), RIVROS (cold), ANAGANTIOS (staying-in), OGRONIOS (cold-time), CVTIOS (windy?), GIAMONIOS (winter-end), SIMIVISONNIOS (bright half), EQVOS (horse), ELEMBIVIOS (deer-time), EDRINIOS (heat), CANTLOS (song?). We read the first two months in full.

lessons.title: The Coligny Calendar, Part Two
lessons.content: The intercalary system. MID (good) and ANMID (not-good) mark lucky and unlucky days. The particle INIS (in) marks entry dates. TRINVXTION SAMO SINDIV (three-night festival of Samo today). We translate the intercalary month MID SAMONII and the annotations for SAMONIOS.

lessons.title: The Larzac Tablet
lessons.content: A lead curse tablet (defixio) from Larzac (Aveyron, France), c. 100 CE. The longest connected Gaulish text outside the calendar. 160 words, written in cursive Latin script. A group of women invoke supernatural forces against another group of women. We read lines 1–10: IN ALCVINOM CANTOBEDNNABOGAITIRCON NOILBINACON NATARCON DAXTECXXTONIAVDEDASETI.

lessons.title: The Larzac Tablet, Continued
lessons.content: Parsing the curse. AVDE (invokes), DAXTECXXTONI (to the lower ones), ADSAXSATILIN (the ones who bind). We identify noun stems, verb forms, and the dative plural ending -bo. This is the hardest text in the corpus.

lessons.title: The Chamalières Tablet
lessons.content: A lead curse tablet from Chamalières (Puy-de-Dôme), c. 50 CE. Found in a sacred spring in 1971. Sixty words. The text invokes MAPONOS ARVERNORIGIIS (Maponos of the Arverni kings). We read the opening: ANDEDION VEDIIUMI DIIIUIOMI RISVM RISVM VEDIIUMÍ AVDMON AVOTÓN.

lessons.title: The Vercelli Stone Bilingual
lessons.content: A funerary stele from Vercelli (Piedmont, Italy), c. 1st century BCE. Written in both Lepontic and Latin. Lepontic: AKANONETIVIS / TANKINOM / IUVINOM. Latin: C. VALERIUS C. F. / ATANIO. The Lepontic text is a dedication in the dative. We parse every word.

lessons.title: Funerary Inscriptions, Part One
lessons.content: Epitaphs from Gaul. The formulae: ANDEDASETI (he set up), BRIXTOM (magic?), MARKOM (horse), MONI (memorial). We read five complete epitaphs from Autun, Alise-Sainte-Reine, and Saint-Marcel.

lessons.title: Funerary Inscriptions, Part Two
lessons.content: The Gaulish genitive. SEGOMARI MATIR (mother of Segomarus), DAXTIONI ATEPOMAROS (Atepomaros son of Daxtio). The common personal names and their components: SEG- (victory), MAR- (great), VER- (over), RIG- (king), DAGO- (good).

lessons.title: Dedicatory Inscriptions
lessons.content: Votive offerings to the gods. LVGVS, ROSMERTA, BELENVS, TARANIS, ESVS. The formula DEDEMIT (he gave), IEVRV (to the sacred place). We read ten complete votives from southern Gaul.

lessons.title: The Gaulish Verb
lessons.content: What we know. Third singular -IT, third plural -ONT, preterite -S. Infinitives and other forms are rare or unattested. The verb DEDEMIT appears in dozens of inscriptions; it is the backbone of Gaulish epigraphy.

checkpoint.title: Stage 2 Checkpoint
checkpoint.format: Written. Translate three passages: one from the Coligny Calendar, one from the Larzac Tablet, one funerary inscription. All with glosses and partial parsing provided. Pass mark: 75%.

capstone_examination.title: The Kalopaideia Diploma in Reading Gaulish Epigraphy
capstone_examination.format: Written examination, auto-graded. Four parts: (1) Translate three previously-prepared inscriptions (one from each major category: calendar, curse tablet, funerary) with notes. (2) Translate one unseen short inscription (ten words or fewer) with a provided glossary. (3) Parse ten inflected forms (noun and verb). (4) Multiple-choice on script identification, phonology, and historical context. Total time: ninety minutes.

certification.credential_name: The Kalopaideia Diploma in Reading Gaulish Epigraphy
certification.credential_subtitle: An attestation that the bearer can read the surviving inscriptions of pre-Roman Gaul with notes.
certification.what_it_is: A privately-issued certificate of completion. This is not an academic degree. It attests that the holder sat down with the Gaulish corpus, learned the scripts, studied the texts, and passed an examination on them.
certification.what_is_recorded: Student's chosen public name; the language; the date of the capstone examination; the result (Pass or Pass with Honors); the SHA-256 hash of the student's signed examination scripts.
certification.what_is_not_recorded: The actual examination answers; the student's email or other identifiers; anything that could identify the student without consent. The certificate is pseudonymous if the student wishes.
certification.issuance: On-chain on Base (Ethereum L2) as an ERC-721 soulbound (non-transferable) token. One certificate per student per language. The contract is owned by Kalopaideia and the minting key is held by the proprietor. The token URI points to a permanent, IPFS-pinned JSON document signed by Kalopaideia's issuing key.
certification.verification: Any third party can verify a certificate at kalopaideia.com/verify/<token-id> by entering the token ID and the certificate hash. The page will display the issuance date, the language, and the result.
certification.cost: Included in the Akousma subscription. The on-chain gas fee at issuance is paid by Kalopaideia. The student pays nothing extra.
certification.first_of_its_kind: The first blockchain-issued credential for a dead Celtic language.

policies.honor_code: All examinations are taken under the Kalopaideia honor code. The student attests, by signing the examination, that no aid was used beyond the materials permitted in the examination instructions. A student found in breach forfeits the right to be examined again for one calendar year.
policies.retakes: A failed checkpoint may be retaken after seven days; a failed capstone after thirty days. There is no limit to the number of retakes.
policies.withdrawal: The student may withdraw at any time. Progress is preserved. No refund is offered for the subscription, which is month-to-month.
policies.accommodations: The capstone may be taken in untimed form for any student who requests it.
